title: Verifier‑Grounded Generate‑Verify‑Repair for Intent‑to‑Configuration NetOps Tasks: A Paired Mininet Emulation Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a provenance‑traced paired confirmatory study (N = 200 intents; 400 paired episodes) to evaluate whether a deterministic verifier‑grounded generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop reduces operationally detectable policy‑violation errors when a hosted LLM produces device configuration sequences from operator intent in a Mininet emulation. Execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one sampled initial generation per intent reused by both baseline and guarded). Baseline success (no detected policy violation) = 196/200 (98%); guarded success = 200/200 (100%). Paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.02; preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.125 (primary confirmatory test). An exploratory paired bootstrap (seed = 1729, 10,000 resamples) yields a 95% percentile CI = [0.005, 0.04]. Four verifier‑triggered repairs occurred (total hosted model calls = 204), giving mean extra model calls per intent = 0.02 and mean extra calls per avoided violation = 1.0. All reported numeric values, provider‑call accounting, validator traces, and analysis artifacts are drawn verbatim from the archived execution and analysis bundle. We interpret the preregistered confirmatory result conservatively and discuss construct, internal, and external validity limits and operational implications.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation is a promising NetOps automation vector but raises operational safety questions because large language models (LLMs) can produce mechanically detectable faults—syntax errors, topology/reachability violations, and ACL/policy mistakes—that may cause availability loss or unintended access [1], [4]. A common mitigation pattern is a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline that pairs an LLM generator with a deterministic verifier capable of checking mechanizable constraints and, when violations occur, requesting localized repairs from the model [2], [3]. Previous prototype work demonstrates that verifier‑guided repair can reduce mechanically checkable errors in code and domain‑specific program generation, yet empirical evidence across heterogeneous multi‑vendor templates and audited hosted‑LLM cost accounting remains limited [4], [5], [2].

We preregistered and executed study C1‑GVR‑multivendor‑2026‑v1 to quantify whether a deterministic verifier plus a bounded repair budget reduces operationally detectable policy‑violation errors in a controlled Mininet emulation. The design is paired and provenance‑traced: for each intent we produced exactly one sampled initial LLM candidate that was reused by both baseline and guarded episodes (shared_initial_candidate semantics). Under this semantics the baseline outcome is the validator's assessment of the shared initial candidate; the guarded outcome is the final guarded pipeline result after deterministic validation and any permitted repair. This design isolates the effect of deterministic verification/repair from differences in first‑pass sampling or prompt templates. All experimental artifacts, provider accounting, and verifier traces are archived and cited in the preregistration and execution manifests; all reported quantitative values below are taken verbatim from those artifacts.
sections.related_work:
Surveys and domain reviews document rapid growth in LLM‑for‑NetOps and AIOps research and emphasize recurring gaps: benchmark provenance, verifier integration, and limited multi‑vendor emulation evidence [5], [6]. NetOps‑specific prototypes show that LLMs can draft device configurations but commonly introduce syntactic or topology errors that require deterministic checking to detect and correct [4], [1]. Across adjacent domains, verifier‑grounded closed loops (GVR) have been proposed and evaluated in prototype studies for code and domain programs where a mechanistic verifier (compiler, interpreter, or formal checker) supplies localized diagnostics used to solicit model repairs; results indicate that verifier feedback can materially reduce mechanically checkable failures when the verifier's coverage aligns with the failure modes of interest [2], [3].

This study builds on those findings by (i) applying a provenance‑traced paired confirmatory design across heterogeneous synthetic vendor templates in a Mininet emulator, (ii) using shared_initial_candidate semantics so paired differences derive solely from verifier/repair actions, and (iii) reporting audited provider and stage accounting to quantify repair cost in concrete hosted‑LLM call counts. We avoid claims of production readiness and position the work as an artifact‑grounded proof‑of‑concept within a tightly specified scope.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: We preregistered the study as C1‑GVR‑multivendor‑2026‑v1 before any model calls (preregistration SHA‑256 = 9e0fc992665835975b01289f7841926ef6abf3584252c5d0459ba0ecf166bb50). The primary confirmatory estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (probability that an intent yields zero operationally detectable violations under guarded minus baseline) tested using the exact McNemar two‑sided test (α = 0.05). Exploratory estimators predeclared include a paired bootstrap percentile confidence interval for the paired risk difference (bootstrap_seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000) and descriptive cost metrics (mean extra hosted model calls per intent and mean extra calls per avoided violation). The preregistration specified sample size N = 200 paired intents (planned episodes = 400) with stratified deterministic selection across three vendor‑template families and four topology patterns (12 strata).

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and inferential meaning: Execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each intent exactly one initial sampled LLM candidate was created and reused by both baseline and guarded episodes. Under this execution contract baseline outcomes equal the validator's score on that identical initial candidate; guarded outcomes reflect the final pipeline after deterministic validation and any allowed repair. The preregistration explicitly declared that independent constrained‑prompt arms were not executed; therefore any paired difference arises solely from verifier detection and repair, not from different first‑pass samples or prompt modifications.

Model, sampling marker, and budget: The declared hosted model in archived execution artifacts is gpt‑5‑mini (provider recorded as openai_responses). The archived model_configuration.json records temperature = null/unset; we state explicitly that null/unset is not evidence of deterministic provider sampling and does not imply temperature = 0. Planned budgets were initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1 and maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1, with a global maximum_model_calls budget = 400.

Deterministic validator, scoring rule, and repair policy: The verifier used (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) implements layered checks: syntactic parsing of configuration commands, required‑command sequencing (order and presence), topology/reachability validation against the emulated network state, and encoded ACL/policy checks derived from the per‑task payload constraints. The preregistered scoring rule full_intent_constraint_validation returns a boolean success flag (no detected violations) when all required commands appear, sequencing constraints are satisfied, topology invariants hold, and protected interfaces remain untouched. When the validator reports violations the guarded pipeline was permitted up to one verifier‑triggered repair call that reused localized diagnostics to construct a repair prompt requesting targeted corrections. Repair calls were issued only when the validator returned violations and were limited to one per intent by the preregistered contract.

Sampling plan, exclusions, and missingness rules: Tasks were deterministically selected by the adapter's task_index_profile before any model calls. Exclusion rules in the preregistration allowed removal of duplicate tasks or pairs aborted due to infrastructure failures; ambiguous validator outputs were conservatively treated as failures in the primary analysis. In execution no pairs were excluded and no episodes failed; missingness summary from analysis artifacts reports complete_pairs = 200 and failed episodes = 0.

Deterministic accounting and provider audit: The execution manifest audited hosted_model_call_event_count = 204 decomposed as 200 shared_initial_generation events and 4 repair calls. Cache statistics show cache_hit_count = 0 and cache_miss_count = 204. Stage accounting reports shared_initial_generation = 200 and repair stage = 4. These audited counts are preserved in the execution and deterministic_reconciliation artifacts and reported verbatim in Results to enable reproducibility reconciliation.
sections.results:
Execution completeness and raw contingency: The run completed per preregistration: planned_episode_count = 400; completed_episode_count = 400; complete_pair_count = 200; failed_episode_count = 0. The paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is n11 = 196, n10 = 4, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Baseline success rate = 196/200 = 0.98; guarded success rate = 200/200 = 1.0; paired point estimate (guarded − baseline) = 0.02.

Confirmatory test and exploratory interval: The preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test on the paired binary outcomes returns p = 0.125 (primary confirmatory result; do not reject at α = 0.05). The archived exploratory paired bootstrap (bootstrap_seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000) produced a 95% percentile CI for the paired risk difference = [0.005, 0.04]. Both the McNemar test result and the bootstrap computation (seed and resamples) are recorded in the analysis artifacts. We caution that when discordant pair counts (n10 + n01) are small, bootstrap percentile intervals can be unstable; the preregistered exact McNemar remains the formal confirmatory inference under our design.

Repair accounting and cost tradeoff: Four verifier‑triggered repairs were invoked across the 200 intents. Total hosted model calls = 204 (200 shared initial + 4 repair calls), yielding mean hosted model calls per intent = 1.02 and mean extra calls per intent due to repairs = 0.02. Each repair corrected one baseline failure in the archived contingency, hence mean extra calls per avoided violation = 1.0 under the observed outcomes. These arithmetic derivations follow directly from the audited provider_call counts in the execution_manifest and deterministic_reconciliation artifacts.

Representative episodes and validator traces: Representative per‑episode artifacts (scorer/validator traces archived for sample tasks) show identical shared_initial_candidate content reused by both baseline and guarded conditions and show validator_trace.validation_before documenting detected violations and validator_trace.validation_after recording repair_applied and subsequent success for the discordant pairs. Examination of representative entries confirms that repaired episodes transitioned from violation_present before repair to valid after repair under the deterministic validator's checks.

Statistical diagnostics and power interpretation: The preregistered power plan targeted detection of a 10 percentage point absolute reduction with N ≈ 157 (McNemar approximation); N = 200 was chosen to allow stratified descriptions. The observed baseline failure prevalence (2%) is lower than some planning scenarios and yields small discordant counts (4), which reduces power to detect small absolute improvements and increases sampling variability of resampling intervals. This accounts for the observed non‑significant McNemar despite a positive point estimate and motivates cautious interpretation of exploratory intervals.
sections.discussion:
Meaning of findings under shared_initial_candidate semantics: Because the experiment used shared_initial_candidate semantics, the baseline condition and the guarded condition initially observed precisely the same LLM sample per intent; consequently any paired improvement arises only from deterministic validator detection and the permitted repairs. The preregistration explicitly forbade independent first‑pass re‑sampling for the paired comparison; therefore the study measures the marginal effect of deterministic verifier/repair, not the combined effect of constrained prompting or multi‑sample selection.

Operational implications (bounded): Within the constrained Mininet emulation, synthetic vendor templates, and the validator's rule coverage, a small repair budget (four repairs) removed the mechanically detectable baseline violations at low model‑call overhead. This artifact‑grounded outcome suggests that when a deterministic verifier can express relevant constraints and provide localized diagnostics, limited repair budgets can correct template‑driven mechanically checkable faults in similar emulated settings. We explicitly do not claim generalization to production hardware, other prompt families, different LLMs, or to semantic errors outside the validator's formalized rule set.

Threats to validity (expanded): Construct validity—the deterministic validator covers syntax, required sequencing, reachability, and encoded ACL/policy rules but cannot detect higher‑order semantic misinterpretations not expressible in those checks; residual false negatives remain a primary construct threat. Internal validity—the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics were implemented and verified in the deterministic_reconciliation artifact, eliminating differential sampling as a confound. Conclusion validity—small discordant counts limit inferential power and resampling stability; the exact McNemar test is the preregistered confirmatory procedure and should be emphasized when discordant counts are sparse. External validity—single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini), synthetic templates, and Mininet emulation limit extrapolation to real production environments and multi‑model robustness.

Recommendations grounded in archived evidence: (1) Expand verifier coverage to include richer semantic and policy ontologies and instrument verifier false‑negative estimation via injection tests; (2) perform paired designs that allow independent multi‑sample initial generations per condition to isolate prompt and sampling effects (not executed here); (3) evaluate multiple hosted models and versions to measure sensitivity to provider nondeterminism and sampling configuration; (4) preserve provenance tracing for every provider call and validator trace to enable external audit and reproducibility; (5) report audited provider accounting (hosted_model_call_event_count and decomposition) as part of operational cost statements. Each recommendation follows directly from observed artifact evidence and limitations recorded in the preregistration and execution manifest.

Reviewer‑requested clarifications addressed here: We explicitly state that model_configuration.json recorded temperature = null/unset and that null/unset does not imply temperature = 0; we clarify shared_initial_candidate semantics and inferential consequences; we report audited provider_call accounting verbatim (hosted_model_call_event_count = 204 decomposed as 200 initial + 4 repair calls) and explain how stage_counts map to the shared design; and we add an explicit caution about bootstrap CI behavior with small discordant counts. The immutable initial master prompt locator and its SHA‑256 are preserved in the Disclosure Statement below, as required.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a provenance‑traced paired confirmatory study (N = 200 intents; shared_initial_candidate semantics) to measure whether a deterministic verifier plus bounded repair reduces mechanically detectable policy violations for intent→configuration tasks in a Mininet emulation. The preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test did not reject at α = 0.05 (p = 0.125). Guarded GVR invoked four repairs and corrected the four observed baseline violations at low model‑call overhead (mean extra calls per intent = 0.02), yielding a paired risk difference estimate of 0.02 and an exploratory paired bootstrap CI = [0.005, 0.04] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10,000). These artifact‑grounded results indicate that when a deterministic verifier can express and check relevant constraints and provide localized feedback, a small repair budget can eliminate mechanically detectable policy violations in similar template‑based emulated settings. The results do not establish production readiness, multi‑model generality, or coverage for semantic errors outside the validator. Future preregistered, provenance‑traced evaluations should expand verifier coverage, evaluate multiple hosted models, and compare independent multi‑sample baselines.

disclosure_statement: Declared model: gpt‑5‑mini (provider recorded as openai_responses). Adapter/adapter family: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Task generator: deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Preregistration: C1‑GVR‑multivendor‑2026‑v1 (SHA‑256 = 9e0fc992665835975b01289f7841926ef6abf3584252c5d0459ba0ecf166bb50) was recorded before any model calls. Initial master prompt archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Human role: a human Research Director selected the topic family and constrained the initial master prompt prior to the autonomy lock; after the lock the AI autonomously performed literature verification, preregistration, experiment execution, analysis, peer review, revision, and manuscript drafting; no human manually edited technical manuscript content after the autonomy lock. Sampling semantics: execution used shared_initial_candidate (one sampled initial generation per intent was produced and reused by both baseline and guarded); archived model configuration records temperature = null/unset (null/unset is not evidence of deterministic provider sampling and does not imply temperature = 0). Provider accounting (audited): hosted_model_call_event_count = 204 decomposed as 200 shared initial generations + 4 repair calls. Reported numbers and analysis artifacts are drawn from the archived execution and analysis bundles.
limitations: Scope limited to Mininet‑style emulation with synthetic, provenance‑traced intent→configuration tasks; results do not generalize directly to production hardware or live operations.
Single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) evaluated; multi‑model generality is not established.

Deterministic validator coverage limited to mechanically checkable errors (syntax, reachability, ACL/policy encodings); higher‑level semantic or specification misinterpretations outside the validator may remain undetected.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics imply observed paired differences derive only from verifier‑triggered repair; this design does not measure effects of alternative prompting strategies or independent multi‑sample candidate selection.

Observed confirmatory effect (2 percentage points) did not reach statistical significance at α = 0.05 for N = 200 (exact McNemar p = 0.125); low baseline failure prevalence (2%) reduced power to detect small absolute improvements under some preregistered scenarios.
